knowledge: In-house SEs (社内SE) commonly struggle with two problems: superiors and seniors who teach them nothing, and uncertainty about what they should study; these stem from structural conditions around the role rather than individual failings.
IT demand continues to rise and is expected to keep growing, so numerous projects land on in-house SEs and produce chronic resource shortages.

Business companies that employ in-house SEs tend to prioritize projects over internal education; as a result, bosses and seniors must allocate their time to project work and cannot teach even when they want to.

In Japan, in-house SEs are a minority of IT talent: roughly 70 % belong to vendor firms such as SIers and only about 30 % belong to user/business companies. Overseas the ratio is reversed, with most IT professionals employed by user companies.

Because most Japanese IT educational materials are written for SIers, they do not fit in-house SE work well; readers often feel that books contain useful fragments yet never quite match their actual job.
The spread of remote work has reduced informal workplace learning: fewer chances exist to watch seniors work or to pick up knowledge through casual conversation.
First-year in-house SEs (社内SE 1年生) are simultaneously first-year working adults and therefore have a large volume of things to learn.

Surrounding information overflow makes it easy to become lost about where to start, so efficient learning that actually produces results requires first understanding the knowledge and skills especially demanded of a first-year in-house SE and acquiring those items preferentially.
To identify those priority items it is necessary to understand what is expected of a first-year in-house SE.
The expectation placed on a first-year in-house SE is defined as equal to the necessary knowledge and skills.
The background that generates those expectations consists of three layers: the current state of Japanese business, the IT expectations held by operating (non-IT) companies, and global IT trends.
Chapter 1 is framed as answering two core questions: what kind of occupation an in-house SE actually is, and how the in-house SE role will evolve in the future.
We are currently in the midst of the 4th Industrial Revolution.

In the 20th century's 3rd Industrial Revolution, the emergence of PCs and the Internet began the automation of work previously performed by people, centered on manufacturing. Systems such as ERP packages were introduced to improve on-site work efficiency, and in-house SEs (社内SE) started their role in promoting their company's IT adoption.

In the 21st century, the 4th Industrial Revolution uses digital technologies (IoT, big data, AI, etc.) to connect things to the Internet and achieve optimization. Devices such as home appliances, automobiles, and factory equipment connect to the Internet, collect data, and can be controlled via smartphones.

IT utilization has permeated not only business but every domain. In-house SEs expanded their contribution beyond previous ERP and other business systems to also supporting external service provision that uses digital technologies.

Some corporate executives have shifted from the idea of introducing IT into business toward IT-centric management (IT経営), in which management is considered with IT as the axis. Examples include EC players such as Amazon and Rakuten, which do not treat IT as a mere tool or means but develop strategies and business models premised on IT.

The globally progressing industrial revolution has spread the necessity of IT not only to business but to society as a whole. In this major trend, the in-house SE is precisely the presence that is needed.
Some voices claim that we have already entered the 5th Industrial Revolution, but this book omits that discussion.
The term '4th Industrial Revolution' is said to have originated from 'Industrie 4.0,' proposed by Germany at Hannover Messe 2011.

Following a triggering declaration, countries launched national 4th Industrial Revolution programs: Germany 2011 Industrie 4.0 (public-private manufacturing automation involving Bosch and Siemens, digitalizing government/industry/society); UK 2011 Catapult Centres (IoT-driven innovation especially in life and energy); USA 2011 Advanced Manufacturing Partnership (GE, IBM, Intel promoting internet-enabled services); China 2015 Made in China 2025 (IT to raise manufacturing standards, IT-based production foundations and digitally controlled robots); Japan 2015 Japan Revitalization Strategy promoting Society 5.0 (super-smart society) covering both corporate 4th Industrial Revolution and individual lifestyle change, aiming for comfortable, affluent living across production, distribution, sales, transport, health/medical, finance and public services.
Global 4th Industrial Revolution statements and programs acted as a tailwind for IT; the COVID-19 pandemic from 2019 further accelerated digitalization.
In Japan, digitalization had been driven mainly by large firms; the pandemic shifted IT/digitalization from ‘necessary’ to ‘inevitable,’ prompting SMEs to begin digital transformation.
Internal SEs (社内SE) sit inside this global IT-utilization trend and the occupation is expected to see solid, continuing demand growth, making it an attractive career.
Japan's rapid declining birthrate and aging population (少子高齢化) is a key factor uniquely accelerating IT and digitalization in the country.

Japan's total population peaked in December 2004 at 127.84 million people and has been declining since, representing a historic turning point heading toward population levels of about 100 years earlier.
Systems built on the assumption of population growth—such as social welfare and pensions—are being forced to change due to this demographic shift.
Existing business models and ways of working are also under strong pressure to transform, with IT technology playing a critical supporting role.

According to the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry (METI) 'Basic Survey on Overseas Business Activities,' the overseas production ratio of Japan's manufacturing sector as a whole rose from 6.4% in FY1990 to 13.4% in FY2000.

Long-term population data (based on Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications statistics): Meiji Restoration (1868) population was 33.3 million; end of WWII (1945) was 71.99 million; 2100 projection is 47.71 million with an aging rate of 40%.
The graph of Japan's population dynamics shows a peak-out followed by a steep decline after 2004.

Japan's business environment features shrinking domestic resources driven by declining birthrate, aging population, and other complex factors, while global markets expand. For companies operating borderless businesses, IT is indispensable for efficiently exchanging information globally and supporting operations.

World IT trends together with Japan's demographic change and globalization are expanding expectations of IT. As a result, expectations of internal SEs (社内SE) who support corporate IT from within are also changing.
Internal SEs must themselves change in response to these shifts in the environment surrounding them.
Ability to change varies among people. Those who have long succeeded as traditional internal SEs often find past success experiences obstruct necessary change.

First-year internal SEs should recognize that some seniors and colleagues have not changed (or cannot change), while still drawing on company training and seniors' knowledge, thinking independently, and absorbing what they need.
Core guidance: internal SEs must also change; when absorbing knowledge, deliberately consider 'what to learn and from whom.'

Relevant contextual factors include the current state of Japanese business, operating companies' expectations of IT, and global IT trends, along with the distinction between people who have adapted and those who have not.

A company's degree of IT promotion acceleration can be understood from its attitude toward IT investment and the ratio of investment amount to profit.

Even for a first-year in-house SE (社内SE 1年生), the company's IT investment enthusiasm greatly affects the size of opportunities they will experience: proactive IT investment yields many challenge opportunities, while a lack of it can limit opportunities.
First-year in-house SEs need to understand their IT department's current state, direction, and how hard the company is pressing the accelerator (アクセルの踏み具合).

IT investment amount ratio (IT投資額比率) is sometimes used as a measure; it is generally said to be 1% of sales, though industry, business type, and company growth lifecycle (growth, maturity, decline) make uniform judgment difficult—this remains a useful guideline.
To grasp an IT department's direction, distinguish traditional IT investment from new IT investment; high total IT spend does not automatically mean the company is aggressive about new IT.
Investment area is one indicator of whether there is expectation or appetite for new IT, also called offensive IT (攻めのIT).

Traditional IT investment vs. offensive IT investment (攻めのIT投資): Purpose — cost reduction vs. increasing sales and added value; Tendency — safety-first vs. speed-first; Target area — backend vs. frontend; Style — mostly waterfall vs. mostly Agile and DevOps.
A company's enthusiasm and willingness to promote IT can be inferred from its organization chart.

When the information systems function exists only as a subsection inside General Affairs (or sometimes Accounting), there is typically no CIO; corporate IT awareness and investment appetite tend to be low.
When a CIO sits at the top of a dedicated IT department, management's clear intent to advance IT is visible; the CIO drives IT strategy and execution from a specialized standpoint.

The internal structure of the IT department further reveals whether the CIO emphasizes offensive (growth-oriented) IT investment or traditional (maintenance) IT investment. Presence of a DX promotion organization, for example, signals an active intent to pursue offensive IT.

Knowing this difference lets an in-house SE understand what can versus cannot be learned inside the company: gaps should be filled by external information gathering, and strong interest in unobtainable experience may justify considering a future job change.
The book focuses on the basic rules required of first-year in-house SEs, so the skills it teaches remain useful in any workplace—whether the organization is proactive about IT or not.

In-house SEs (社内SE) do not belong to the IT industry; they belong to the industry or sector of their business company (事業会社).
In-house SEs perform their duties with the cooperation of various people from the IT industry and sectors, so understanding the structure of the IT industry is necessary.
The IT industry, like other businesses, consists of B2C and B2B. B2C can be classified as Web-related (Web系) and B2B as SIer-related (SIer系).
Web系 companies are internet firms such as Google, Amazon, and LINE Yahoo that conduct businesses directly related to consumers and therefore tend to have high name recognition.
SIer系 company examples include Hitachi, Nomura Research Institute, and Accenture. They mainly provide contracted system development and consulting services.
In-house SEs are mostly involved in building the IT infrastructure that supports their own company's business, so they primarily interact with SIer-type companies.
The IT industry is classified into five types of businesses (業種). Understanding which types of people from which sectors provide support in which situations is important for advancing IT initiatives.
Internet/Web sector: in-house SE involvement example is utilizing Web services for the company; example companies are Google, Amazon, LINE Yahoo; they provide services using their own websites.
Communications sector: in-house SE involvement example is contracting the company's own network lines; example companies are NTT, SoftBank, KDDI; they provide communication service infrastructure.

Internal SE (社内SE) work is surrounded by three main IT industry segments: package software (contracts with vendors such as Microsoft and Oracle that develop software and provide post-sales support), hardware (server-purchase quotes from vendors such as Hitachi and Toshiba that develop hardware and provide post-sales support), and information-processing services (system-construction projects with firms such as NTT Data and Accenture that deliver planning through operations, contracted development, and consulting).

A business company that employs internal SE uses IT to deliver its own products and services; therefore it either builds the required IT capabilities in-house or procures products and services from the IT-industry players listed above.
Understanding the industry map lets an internal SE know whom to interact with for system development versus whom to contact for hardware purchases.

Key IT job titles that internal SE encounter, together with their core responsibilities: システムエンジニア (System Engineer) designs software and examines program specifications (the term is also used broadly for any IT-related role); ITコンサルタント (IT Consultant) proposes IT-based solutions to business problems; ネットワークエンジニア (Network Engineer) designs, builds and operates networks; セキュリティエンジニア (Security Engineer) handles information-security work; プログラマー (Programmer) writes code from designs and specifications; テスター (Tester) verifies the quality of coded systems; ITプロジェクトマネージャ (IT Project Manager) manages and drives an entire project.

Internal SE need to know these role definitions so that, when they meet people with various titles on a project, they can correctly anticipate each person’s expected contribution and communicate accordingly.
First-year in-house SEs (社内SE 1年生) must understand not only general system engineer roles but also the distinctions among SIer SE, 社内SE (in-house SE), and SES (System Engineering Service).
SES formally denotes an employment/contract form, but in IT industry custom it commonly refers to SEs stationed at a client site (客先常駐SE).
In typical practice, in-house SEs carry out system construction and operation/maintenance with cooperation from SIer SEs and SES; the exact arrangement depends on project scale and company culture.
New system development is frequently commissioned to SIer SEs.
Enhancements of existing systems are often advanced by consulting the SIer or SES already responsible for that system's operation and maintenance.
A common large-scale collaboration pattern is: the in-house SE commissions construction to an SIer, and the SIer re-commissions work support to SES.
SIer SE: belongs to an SIer, introduces IT into client companies, and mainly handles upstream processes.
社内SE (in-house SE): belongs to a business company, uses IT to contribute to that company, and covers a wide range from development through operations.
SES: a contract that provides system-engineering as a service; typically a quasi-mandate (準委任契約) employment form; by custom also used to mean a client-stationed SE.
In Japanese IT, an in-house SE (社内SE) typically takes internal business planning and requests systemization from a large SIer rather than building everything internally.

A large SIer acts as the prime contractor (一次請け): it accepts the project, forms a project team, and if it lacks resources it further requests support from external SIers (who may themselves subcontract further).
An SES-providing SIer (SES提供SIer) acts as a subcontractor (二次請け) and supplies personnel as on-site/resident support (常駐支援) according to the requester’s resource needs.
The large SIer’s project team builds the system and, after completion, delivers the product/service to the requesting in-house SE.
After the in-house SE performs acceptance inspection (検収), the business company pays the large SIer under the contract.
Payment from the large SIer to the SES provider is for the contracted support work and is independent of whether the overall system has been completed and delivered (step ④).
The typical collaboration chain is: in-house SE (requester) → large SIer (prime) → SES SIer (subcontractor), illustrated as Figure 1-11.
In-house SE (社内SE) is the IT specialist of a business company and must understand how IT initiatives relate to and contribute to the company's own business.
Direct work areas of an in-house SE are system construction (システム構築), infrastructure construction (インフラ構築), and operations/maintenance (運用保守).
The contribution required of an in-house SE is not introducing the highest-quality system in those work areas, but bringing value to the business through the system.
A first-year in-house SE must understand the link between the company's product/service profit-and-reinvestment cycle and IT investment.
A business company provides products and services to customers based on its vision and mission, thereby realizing social contribution.
Money received from customers in return for products/services is sales (売上). Profit (利益) is sales minus various costs.
Profit is used for retained earnings (内部留保), returns to shareholders, reinvestment, and similar purposes.

Corporate activity and IT investment form a cycle: mission and vision drive corporate strategy, business strategy, and IT strategy; strategy-based investment decisions lead to execution plans and measures; the company delivers products/services to customers, generating sales; costs (including IT investment in hardware and software) are subtracted to yield profit, which is reinvested (including further IT investment).

Companies reinvest a portion of profits according to corporate strategy for business continuity and expansion, aiming at further cost reduction or sales growth. Internal SE work is one such reinvestment process that uses part of those profits.

Corporate reinvestment is a foundation of business. If this is not understood, people wrongly treat the purpose of a project as merely building a system or infrastructure. IT solutions are only one means of achieving business goals.

When improving a business area, options are not limited to introducing a modern solution because the current in-house system is 30 years old; another option is to outsource the business function itself.

First-year internal SEs may find it hard to correctly infer each project's original purpose. Common purposes of projects involving internal SEs, grouped by proposing department, help infer the true aim and the contribution required.

Business (sales) departments typically propose: system modification to acquire new customers; system introduction to launch a new business; system integration accompanying M&A. These often target sales increase.

Operations/business departments typically propose: system modification to improve operational work; new system introduction for efficiency; system modification required by legal/statutory rules. These often target cost reduction or compliance.

IT departments typically propose: response to system aging/obsolescence; hardware update work; security measures. These are often categorized as other (maintenance, risk, or infrastructure) rather than direct sales or cost goals.
Do not misread the original purpose of a project; the system or infrastructure work is a means, not the end.

Two employment models relevant to in-house IT/SE work are job-type employment (ジョブ型雇用) and membership-type employment (メンバーシップ型雇用); understanding them helps predict expected duties and future assignments.

Job-type employment (common overseas, increasingly adopted in Japan) defines roles first and then assigns people who fit those roles. In IT organizations this produces specialists in planning, development, infrastructure, operations, etc.

Membership-type employment (traditional Japanese model) assigns work to people rather than people to predefined jobs. New graduates are hired in bulk and placed where staff are needed; skills are developed through transfers and rotation.

Job-type vs membership-type comparison: job content is limited vs unlimited; hiring is mainly mid-career vs mainly new-graduate bulk hiring; evaluation is based on skills/achievements vs work attitude and tenure; personnel mobility is high vs low.
Job-type firms tend to hire experienced mid-career talent as immediate contributors.

Membership-type employment grows people by giving them varied experience; a key advantage for new in-house SEs is that even those without a strong IT background can accumulate experience and advance, rather than being confined to one specialized domain.
As an in-house SE (社内SE), you can gain broad knowledge and experience; after accumulating that experience, career moves to companies using job-type employment (ジョブ型) or to SIers become possible.

When changing jobs, even for an in-house SE opening, the expected role differs between job-type employment in-house SE and membership-type employment (メンバーシップ型) in-house SE; you must recognize this difference and understand what is expected of you.
This book explains the role of a first-year in-house SE working under membership-type employment.

Chapter 2 covers skills required of an in-house SE; Chapter 3 covers operations/maintenance work (運用保守) that first-year SEs often handle plus project management common to all projects; Chapter 4 onward covers know-how for each phase of system-construction projects.

The people an in-house SE spends the most time with are colleagues and seniors (not SIers or the business departments). Information from them is practical, company-culture-adapted knowledge and know-how based on seniors’ experience and results; learning it helps you contribute in your assigned work.
The person who supplies information and the person who evaluates you are usually the same, so also understanding that person’s expectations tends to connect directly to evaluations.
Internally circulating information becomes obsolete easily because IT technology advances globally day by day; compared with that pace, internal information ages quickly.

From the first year as an in-house SE it is important to understand the characteristics of internal information versus the necessity of external information, and to maintain awareness of scrutiny and information gathering.
The know-how in this book is foundational and therefore less likely to become obsolete, but you still need to keep your antenna out and collect information on the latest IT technologies and trends.
External information gathering is necessary; a recommended resource is the author’s blog IT Comp@ss with the article “社内SE・情シス初心者必見！おすすめ勉強会・研修・セミナー” at https://itinfoshop.com/se-seminar/.

From the organization chart, you can recognize the current state of your company's IT-ization. Understand what is expected from how hard the company is pressing the accelerator on IT promotion, and aim to contribute.
In-house SEs belong to a business company (not an IT vendor). Understand the IT industry and business types, collaborate with SIers, and contribute to deepening the company's IT.

Information circulating inside the company and knowledge from seniors has immediate effectiveness. However, be careful of information becoming obsolete. Also expand antennas for information gathering outside the company and maintain balance.
Due to the Fourth Industrial Revolution and Japan's declining birthrate and aging population, IT demand is increasing and opportunities for in-house SEs to play an active role are expanding.
The scope of in-house SE is changing. IT is no longer only for traditional cost reduction; it is indispensable for sales expansion and creating added value.
IT solutions are one means of accelerating business. In-house SEs need to understand the original purpose of the business and contribute to value creation with IT.
The importance of IT is accelerating with the Fourth Industrial Revolution. Furthermore, the COVID-19 pandemic changed IT-ization from 'necessary' to 'inevitable'.

For first-year in-house SEs (社内SE 1年生), deciding the priority of what to learn first is more important than deciding what to learn, because available study time is finite; they must acquire skills that can be used immediately on the job.
An effective framework for prioritizing skills is the Katz model proposed by American management scholar Robert Katz (ロバート・カッツ). Figure 2-1 adapts the Katz model for first-year in-house SEs.
In-house SE work sits at the intersection of business-department knowledge and IT (業務×IT), distinct from the more purely technical IT skills typical of SIer engineers.
The Katz-derived skill categories are: conceptual skills (コンセプチュアルスキル), management skills (マネジメントスキル), human skills (ヒューマンスキル), and technical skills (テクニカルスキル).

Skill-mix proportions vary by organizational level: top management, middle management, lower management, and knowledge workers; first-year in-house SEs should visualize their own skill-ratio accordingly.
Chapter 2 is designed to answer: What is needed to produce results at work? Which skills should a first-year in-house SE acquire? What are recommended methods for studying IT skills?

To achieve results (成果), both steady skill-up and strategy/tactics on what to prioritize are required; skill-up alone does not produce results if actions do not connect to outcomes or if the skills (tactics) are not useful.
The structure for raising results consists of 成果 (What to achieve), 戦略 (what to prioritize / How), and 戦術 (how to execute).
Supporting elements of that structure include knowledge (知識), skills (スキル), awareness (意識), and attitude (姿勢).
Chapter 2 also covers how to set strategy that actually leads to results, not only skills themselves.
The Katz model’s technical skills, human skills, and conceptual skills are treated as core skill components, with elements first-year in-house SEs (社内SE) can use in the field.
Management skills are touched only briefly, from the viewpoint of tasks a first-year in-house SE might actually be asked to manage.

Chapter 2 topics include: structure for raising results, skill elements, company strategy vs. personal goals, intrinsic motivation, business knowledge, IT certifications, conceptual skills, human skills, and accelerating learning.
Simply raising skills does not lead to results. To raise results efficiently, it is necessary to understand the relationship between skill-up and results.

Strategy has two levels: company/department strategy and individual goals. In organizations, company-wide vision and policies are subdivided from the top of the organizational structure downward. Individual goals consist of deciding what one wants to accomplish.

Motivation consists of extrinsic motivation and intrinsic motivation. Extrinsic motivation maintains motivation through rewards and punishments but tends to be temporary. Dreams and aspirations are intrinsic motivation and are easier to sustain than extrinsic motivation.
Internal/external actions (社内外行動) include seminars and study groups inside and outside the company that lead to learning, as well as regular internal work and projects.
Tactics are the elements that support How, such as knowledge and skills.
All actions executed inside or outside the company become some form of evaluation or experience.

To raise results, action is required. To raise the quality of action, tactics such as knowledge and skills are needed. High-quality action requires both internal and external motivation. To lower the priority of actions that do not lead to results and prioritize actions that do, understanding of personal goals and organizational strategy is required.
The structure for raising results (成果を上げる構図) depicts organizational activities in the upper part and individual activities in the lower part.

成果を効率的に上げる構図 (structure for efficiently raising results) breaks work into linked steps: strategy-based prioritization of internal/external actions, attaching personal motivation to assigned work, acquiring and applying skills, and converting experience/results into learning and evaluation (Figure 2-5).
For a first-year in-house SE (社内SE 1年生), projects and tasks typically come down from a boss; executing them unthinkingly risks spending time on low-impact work or work that should not be done.
Attach your own motive (動機づけ) to incoming work to raise quality; linking work to higher-aspiration motives (夢・志) sustains motivation better than mere rewards/punishments (報酬・罰則).
Skills raise both efficiency and quality of work; they sit under tactics together with knowledge.

Systematize experience (経験を体系化) and turn it into learning through reflection (振り返り); reflection updates aspirations with new values and ways of thinking, while results feed the next strategy and organizational evaluation.

The framework spans organization vs. individual levels: company/department strategy and personal goals; internal/external actions include 定常業務 (routine work), projects, and セミナー・勉強会 (seminars/study groups).
Priority ranking (優先順位) of actions must be derived from strategy so that effort is not wasted on whatever happens to arrive.
Technical skills (テクニカルスキル / 業務遂行能力) are the knowledge and techniques needed to carry out daily work; they are skills that can be immediately applied in the field.

Skill elements of technical skills include: IT industry knowledge (trends, relationships, and services in the IT industry); IT technical skills (application development, infrastructure, operations/maintenance, management, and other knowledge); industry knowledge (specialized knowledge of the industry the company belongs to); business knowledge (knowledge of the internal business area one is responsible for); and business understanding (understanding of business models and similar, needed to support business with IT).
Conceptual skills (コンセプチュアルスキル / 概念化能力) are the skills needed to accurately grasp the essence of things and to effectively overcome issues.

Skill elements of conceptual skills include: logical thinking / ロジカルシンキング (dividing things into cause and effect and understanding them in sequence); critical thinking / クリティカルシンキング (examining from the fundamental “why/そもそも” without being bound by premises or established concepts); lateral thinking / ラテラルシンキング (considering things from a free, broad perspective rather than only one direction); and a multifaceted viewpoint / 多面的視野 (examining from multiple angles).
俯瞰力 is the ability to see the whole from a high (elevated) perspective.
知的好奇心 is the attitude of taking an interest in unknown things and seeking to know them.
探究心 is the attitude of taking interest and digging deeper.
受容性 is the attitude of accepting different values and opinions.
柔軟性 is the attitude of responding flexibly and adaptively to unexpected events.
チャレンジ精神 is the attitude of confronting opaque or uncertain situations.
洞察力 is the ability to infer unseen parts and think about the essence of things.
先見性 is the ability to think by extending the time axis beyond the immediate present.

ヒューマンスキル (human/interpersonal skills) are skills for building and maintaining good human relationships; they are needed to coordinate with various involved people and advance matters in the desired direction.
コミュニケーション力: ability to converse smoothly and convey one's own intentions to others.
ヒアリング力: ability to listen to others' opinions and understand their thinking.
交渉力: ability to move situations in the desired direction through exchange of opinions.
動機づけ: ability to draw out the other person's motivation.
向上心: attitude of taking things positively and aiming higher.
プレゼンテーション力: ability to convey one's ideas and thoughts logically.
リーダーシップ力: ability to lead an organization.
コーチング力: ability to give advice that helps achieve goals.

Management skills combine various elements of technical skills, conceptual skills, and human skills. Management targets are people (ヒト), things (モノ), money (カネ), and information. The higher the position, the larger the managed scope and amounts become, and the more complex the dependencies that must be considered. For a first-year in-house SE, requested management typically covers a limited range of routine work or a project.

For a first-year in-house SE (社内SE 1年生) to achieve results, appropriate goal setting is essential; if set goals have only a shallow connection (紐づき) to corporate strategy, work outputs are unlikely to become recognized achievements or lead to evaluation.
The key to raising results is to understand corporate strategy and organizational goals, grasp their intent, and relate them to one's own dreams and aspirations (夢や志).
Companies conduct business activities as the means to achieve the vision and purpose they have set; they cascade strategy down into goals so that strategy is embodied and actually functions.

First-year in-house SEs commonly face the problem that requests coming down from superiors are abstract and hard to understand; they must therefore think about why such vague requests appear and learn to respond to them.
Goal cascade (from abstract to concrete): 企業戦略 (corporate strategy) → 事業戦略 / IT戦略 (business strategy, IT strategy) → 部門目標 (department goals) → 個人目標 (personal goals).
High-abstraction goals or requests from a superior should be compared against one's own dreams and aspirations and then made concrete as personal goals.
The relationship between corporate strategy and personal goals runs from abstract (ミッション / ビジョン) at the top to concrete personal goals at the bottom (illustrated in Figure 2-9).

Company visions and missions are highly abstract and must be broken down into concrete goals; work assigned by superiors is therefore naturally somewhat abstract compared with personal plans, and the work of turning it into personal goals is healthy.
Align personal-level goals with your supervisor and contribute to the organization through your activities.

If the direction from a supervisor is overly abstract or missing entirely, that is the supervisor's problem, not yours; treat it as a learning opportunity for how you will act when you become a supervisor.
When converting organizational direction into personal goals, combine it with your own dreams and aspirations so that company work also moves you toward the person you want to become.

Example: An organizational goal of replacing an aging warehouse system to guarantee stable operation can become a personal goal of completing the replacement by October; if your three-year aim is to become an expert in warehouse operations, use the same project to study existing warehouse work eagerly.
Without linking the work to a personal aspiration, warehouse-business knowledge does not expand and the effort may remain a simple version-upgrade of the system.
Connecting corporate activities with personal dreams and aspirations produces both results and growth.
Dreams and aspirations are not found by chance; they result from inputting external information and processing it.
If you lack or cannot identify dreams and aspirations, improve input, processing, or both.
Internal experience (observing bosses and seniors) is limited, so actively collect external information to increase input, as noted on page 35.
Personal-goal setting = Input + Process.

The parable of the three bricklayers: a traveler asks three craftsmen stacking bricks what they are doing. The first replies that he is obviously laying bricks; the second says his job is to build a large wall; the third says they are building a great cathedral that will remain in history.
The third bricklayer, who frames the same physical task as contributing to a historic cathedral, is the one expected to work with high awareness, concentration, and future growth.
The difference among the three is motivation (動機づけ): the assigned work is identical, but the motives they attach to it differ.
Linking a high-level intrinsic motive to a task can raise motivation and improve the quality of action.
First-year in-house SE (社内SE) work is often assigned without a clear explanation of meaning or intent, and sometimes with no particular aim at all.
Assigned work itself cannot be changed, but changing one’s interpretation of it can change the situation.
What matters is not waiting for work related to one’s dreams or aspirations, but the habit of attaching a motive to whatever work arrives.
With this mindset, action quality can be raised above that of people who perform the same tasks without attaching any motive.
Motivation has two kinds: intrinsic motivation (内発的動機) and extrinsic motivation (外発的動機); their differences should be understood.
The practical goal is appropriate motivation: using intrinsic motivation to raise the quality of action.

Types of motivation: Intrinsic motivation (内発的動機) arises from internal factors such as dreams, aspirations, and goals; it tends to be sustainable. Extrinsic motivation (外発的動機) arises from external factors such as rewards, evaluations, and penalties; it tends to be temporary.
Linking only to extrinsic motivation is not denied, but also linking intrinsic motivation helps maintain motivation and tends to make work more enjoyable.
Tying high-perspective motivations (like the third bricklayer in the famous story) enables approaching work with higher awareness.

The royal road to raising perspective is accumulating knowledge and experience plus using external information, but first-year in-house SEs lack sufficient knowledge/experience so cannot use this immediately.

Immediately usable thinking methods for first-year in-house SEs to gain high perspective: (1) Multi-faceted viewpoint / bird's-eye view (多面的視野、俯瞰力) — consider not only one's own view but also those of executives, bosses, customers, etc.; imagine how that person would think about the current situation. (2) Abstract thinking (抽象化思考) — capture the essence of things by deliberately stripping away information.
The goal of these methods is to be able to view the work in front of you from a different angle.

Example: A boss requests attendance at a kickoff meeting with an SIer plus sending of minutes. Literal interpretation is just that task. From a project-owner perspective it can be interpreted as participating on Day 1 of building a partnership with the SIer in order to refresh a decades-old business model and system and construct the next-generation business model. The same experience, when viewed from a high-level overview and abstracted, can be interpreted from a much higher perspective.
Technical skills are divided into business knowledge (業務知識) and IT knowledge (IT知識); this section focuses first on business knowledge.
Required business knowledge differs by the industry and business type of the company you belong to.

In a manufacturing company that designs products in-house, manufactures them, and sells them, there are two main process axes: the Engineering Chain (product design and development) and the Supply Chain (procurement of parts, manufacturing, and sales).
It is first necessary to understand the overall picture of one's own company's business processes.
Typical manufacturing flow: products are planned and measures are considered; once they become sellable, mass production is started at the manufacturing site.
Engineering Chain processes include product planning (製品企画), R&D (研究開発), prototyping/mass production (試作／量産), and maintenance (保守).
Supply Chain processes include production (生産), procurement (調達), logistics (物流), sales (販売), and service (サービス).

Key enterprise systems and their expansions: PLM = Product Lifecycle Management; PDM = Product Data Management; MES = Manufacturing Execution System; CRM = Customer Relationship Management; SCM = Supply Chain Management; ERP = Enterprise Resources Planning.
PLM and PDM primarily support the Engineering Chain; MES, CRM, SCM, and ERP primarily support the Supply Chain.
Acquiring business-process knowledge enables contribution to the business.

New in-house SEs (systems engineers) should understand the overall sense of company operations, typically covered in onboarding/orientation, plus common management techniques frequently encountered in system construction.

CRM (Customer Relationship Management) is a method that aims to expand sales and improve profitability by raising customer satisfaction and customer loyalty. Example vendors: Oracle, Microsoft, Salesforce, Adobe.

ERP (Enterprise Resources Planning) is a method that integrally manages the entire enterprise from the standpoint of effective use of management resources in order to improve management efficiency. Example vendors: SAP, Intuit, Oracle.

MRP (Material Requirements Planning) is a production-management method used in factories. Expanding that concept to cover all manufacturing resources besides materials (personnel, equipment) as well as inventory, settlement, and assets produced ERP.
PLM (Product Lifecycle Management) is a method for centrally managing a product’s entire lifecycle. Example vendors: Siemens, SAP, Dassault.

SCM (Supply Chain Management) is a management method that centrally manages and optimizes product development, procurement, production/processing, inventory management, distribution, and sales. Example vendors: OMP, Kinaxis, o9 Solutions, Blue Yonder.

The main difficulty of IT skill learning for in-house SEs (社内SE) is the scarcity of teaching materials that perfectly fit them, because most Japanese SEs belong to SIers, so SE-oriented materials are mostly aimed at SIer SEs.
In-house SEs need both business and IT skills; they can still skill up by effectively utilizing SIer-SE-oriented learning materials.
One recommended method is to study along SE-oriented IT qualifications (IT資格).
Advantages of learning via qualifications: abundant prepared teaching materials exist for exam preparation; qualifications can be advantageous in future job changes depending on the target company.
SE-oriented IT qualifications fall into three categories: national qualifications (国家資格), vendor qualifications (ベンダー資格), and private qualifications (民間資格).
National qualifications: administered by the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry (経済産業省); characteristic is acquisition of general IT knowledge.
Vendor qualifications: administered by vendors such as AWS or Microsoft Azure; specialized in particular domains and immediately usable on the job.
Private qualifications: occupy an intermediate position between national and vendor qualifications; certified by private vendor-neutral organizations (example: Linux LPIC).
A representative list of qualifications is shown in Figure 2-13; the recommended approach is to start from foundational IT skills and then move to those used in one's own company.
For in-house SEs (社内SE), studying vendor certifications for the cloud or SaaS products actually used by the company is an efficient way to build relevant skills.
If the company's cloud services are unknown, AWS and Microsoft Azure certifications are recommended because those two platforms together cover roughly 60% of the cloud market share.
National (Japan) qualifications worth studying include the Fundamental Information Technology Engineer Examination (基本情報技術者試験) and the Project Manager Examination (プロジェクトマネージャ試験).

There are no mandatory qualifications for in-house SEs. The goal is knowledge and skill acquisition; obtain certifications as a byproduct of studying rather than making certification the purpose. Do not let the means become the end.

IT qualifications can be classified along a 基礎 (basic) vs 応用 (applied) axis and grouped into three types: ユーザー系国家資格 (user-oriented national qualifications), ベンダー資格 (vendor qualifications), and 技術系国家資格 (technical national qualifications).
User-oriented national qualifications include: ITパスポート (IT Passport), プロジェクトマネージャ (Project Manager), ITストラテジスト (IT Strategist), and システム監査技術者 (Systems Auditor).
Vendor qualifications include: AWS認定資格, ORACLE MASTER, Oracle認定Javaプログラマ, GCP (Google Cloud Platform) 認定資格, CCNA (Cisco Certified Network Associate), and Microsoft Azure認定資格.

Technical national qualifications include: 基本情報技術者 (Fundamental Information Technology Engineer), データベーススペシャリスト (Database Specialist), ネットワークスペシャリスト (Network Specialist), システムアーキテクト (Systems Architect), 情報セキュリティマネジメント (Information Security Management), and 応用情報技術者 (Applied Information Technology Engineer).

Five conceptual skills especially recommended for first-year in-house SEs (社内SE): logical thinking (ロジカルシンキング), critical thinking (クリティカルシンキング), lateral thinking (ラテラルシンキング), multi-faceted perspective (多面的視野), and bird's-eye/overview ability (俯瞰力).
These skills are particularly effective because in-house SE work requires daily problem-solving of company business challenges, system failures, and user dissatisfaction.
Problem-solving with conceptual skills involves organizing and analyzing situations, then generating countermeasures from various angles.

Example application: when data does not appear on a system screen, lateral thinking and multi-faceted perspective reframe the event so causes are not limited to system bugs but also include user mistakes and other factors.
Even a single error can be examined multi-facetedly to surface multiple possible causes.
Critical thinking, abstraction thinking, and logical thinking are then used to drill down to root causes; combining them with lateral thinking also allows organizing causes along different time axes.

Although deep analysis benefits from prior experience, understanding how to apply conceptual skills still enables examining events from many angles and manipulating the level of abstraction to aid investigation.
In the illustrated case (Figure 2-14), candidate causes of a 'system bug' issue include AWS outages and application defects as well as other factors.

After using data-problem analysis and multifaceted thinking to surface issues, identify implementation mistakes based on facts. Dig into their causes with multifaceted thinking: the assignee’s quality NG, insufficient testing, and development communication mistakes. Combine this with logical thinking and the present–past–future cut to specify what actions should be taken.

A simple way to raise conceptual skill is to imitate people (inside or outside the company) who think exceptionally well—a lightweight version of a multifaceted viewpoint. Infer their thinking from their statements; after you have thought through a problem yourself, ask “How would that person think?” Increasing the number of such models you imitate makes thinking more multifaceted.

Training conceptual skill (図2-14) links visible phenomena (e.g., data not reflected on screen) to candidate causes such as data problems, app defects, AWS outages, system bugs, user input mistakes, insufficient training, misreading, personnel change, insufficient testing, assignee quality NG, implementation mistakes, missed requirements, and design/development communication mistakes.

Actions are organized by time: present (resolve the event, re-test, investigate and fix locations similar to the found defect, discover latent bugs); past (reflect); future (improve development/test quality, address management and governance issues).
The thinking toolkit associated with these issues includes lateral thinking, multifaceted viewpoint, bird’s-eye view (俯瞰力), logical thinking, and critical thinking.
In-house SEs (社内SE) collaborate with many people and must build good human relationships to proceed with work enjoyably; human skills (ヒューマンスキル) are essential.
Communication skills (コミュニケーション力) and hearing/listening skills (ヒアリング力) are immediately practical skill elements of human skills.
For first-year in-house SEs, the most effective human-skill elements to grasp are customer perspective (顧客視点) and respect toward the other party (相手への敬意).
Example scenario: immediately after a system release, a failure occurs; the business department is furious and the SIer is confused.

Case using only communication and hearing skills: calm the angry business department and learn they treat the issue as a failure because it differs from initially assumed functions; hear the SIer's view that they performed acceptance testing and agreed on the functions, so it is as specified rather than a failure; the in-house SE then mediates so both sides can communicate.
Handling the situation via communication and hearing is possible, but that approach still lacks customer perspective (顧客視点).
Human skills for first-year in-house SEs are framed as using customer perspective to make human relationships smoother.

In incident handling, prioritize preventing inconvenience to the company's customers over debating whether something is a defect or working as specified. Stakeholders should discuss and implement temporary countermeasures first (止血 / stopping the bleeding); discussions between the business department and the SIer come after that.
A customer perspective clarifies what is truly essential, rather than merely mediating between parties who are present.
Focusing too much on communication and hearing tends to overvalue the opinions of people in front of you, so the customer's viewpoint is easily lost.

Projects involve many stakeholders. As one's skills rise, one can become tossed around by those skills; before that happens, one must deliberately listen to the voice of the customer who is not present and cannot speak.
Amazon sometimes leaves one empty seat in a meeting room as a reminder not to forget the customer perspective.
A core human skill to acquire from the first year as a working adult is the attitude of paying respect to others (相手への敬意).

Do not form the habit of deciding how politely to treat someone based on their age or job title. If you do, you will be unable to show respect to juniors once you yourself become older or higher-ranking.
Job titles are almost useless outside that particular company. The portable skill of treating anyone equally, regardless of status, enriches one's life more.

Konosuke Matsushita: everyone is a diamond in the rough; one should pay respect and treat people without regard to position or status. This is especially important to keep in mind as a first-year in-house SE.
Socrates taught that a person is not determined by talent alone, but by the product of talent × education × training (才能×教育×訓練).
Without training, talent and education are not versatile enough to be effectively utilized.
Education is relatively passive learning, while training can be reinterpreted as effort (努力) and is self-directed (spontaneous) learning; this self-directed learning leads to growth.
First-year in-house SEs (社内SE 1年生) are typically too busy to make time for study, so efficient methods for creating time and studying are needed.

To make time for learning, first stop doing something: before starting anything new, decide what to quit. Even apparently idle time is filled with activities (games, drinking tea, zoning out); learning requires creating time by stopping something else.

Start acting while thinking: the main obstacle is taking the first step. Overthinking the future leads to hesitation. Accept being a 'three-day monk' (三日坊主); three days of effort is still progress compared with doing nothing. Repeating a three-day effort 100 times amounts to roughly one year of training.
Necessary actions for learning (図2-15): (1) stop something to make time, (2) think while acting, (3) turn it into a habit. Training/effort is essential; first create time in order to learn.
If the risk of acting and then quitting is acceptable, act first and think about the next action while acting; planning to think first then act often prevents any action from happening.

Habits are system (mechanism) construction: design a learning system by embedding habits into a day or week (e.g., borrow and read library books Monday morning; do a weekly review and systematization Friday evening). Once the system exists, wait for the intended results; design your own behavior.

Habit-formation timeframes: behavioral habits (reading, etc.) ~1 month of continuation; physical habits (quitting smoking, etc.) ~3 months; thinking habits (positive thinking, etc.) ~6 months. Start even as a 'three-day monk' and target 1 month of continuation.

Reflection plus systematization yields more experience from the same event: the experience can be re-lived and turned into generalizable knowledge that applies to similar situations. Abstract thinking extracts the essence of the experience with generality in mind.

Illustration (Fig. 2-16): a person who only experiences an action gets 10 experience points; a person who reflects and systematizes gets 20 from the same 10, with higher output generality. Experience is reused to raise experience value.
業務のテクニカルスキルは、自社ビジネスや業務プロセスの理解で取得できる。
課題解決にはコンセプチュアルスキルが有効。様々な思考方法で課題分析、打ち手の検討ができる。
学ぶ時間は何かをやめなければ生まれない。継続して学ぶことは重要だが、それよりも三日坊主でも始めることはもっと重要。
社内SEにはテクニカル（業務、IT）、コンセプチュアル、ヒューマン、マネジメントの各スキルが必要。
ITのテクニカルスキルは、IT資格にそった勉強で取得するのが効率的。ただし、社内SEは資格取得が必須ではない。
一般的なヒューマンスキルの他に、社会人1年生は「顧客視点」と「相手への敬意」が特に重要。
自社の戦略とアラインした目標設定と仕事の優先順位付けで、企業への貢献と個人の成長の両方を狙う。
社内SE 1年生が貢献するためには、会社員としての必要業務と社内SEとしての業務をソツなくこなせるようになる必要がある。
会社員としての業務は勤怠申請・経費精算・目標管理などで、どの仕事でも必要なため本書では割愛される。
社内SEとしての業務は、定常業務・プロジェクト業務に共通するものとチーム個別のものに分かれる。
社内SE 1年生の基礎業務にはアプリケーション知識・インフラ知識などが含まれる。
社内SE業務の柱として運用保守とプロジェクトマネジメントがある。
第3章で解決できる疑問：社内SEの業務の全体感は何か、運用保守業務は何をすればよいか、プロジェクトマネジメントは何をすることか。

Internal SE work can be classified into two types: team-specific duties that depend on the assigned team, and common duties that are independent of the team (steady operations and project-common work).
Team-specific examples: a system development team may handle management of introduced packages; an infrastructure team may handle cloud- and network-related work.
Chapter 3 focuses on team-independent operations/maintenance (運用保守) and project management, not on team-specific system development or infrastructure construction.

Operations/maintenance and project management can be performed with relatively broad and shallow experience and knowledge, so first-year internal SEs are often assigned to them; they function as a gateway (登竜門) for new internal SEs.

Common organizational areas around this work include help desk (reception window), education/audit, budget-actuals and asset management, development/construction projects, security, and infrastructure management.

Chapter topics in this area include: operations/maintenance work and its opportunities; project management; progress management; WBS; resource management; budget management; issue management; communication management; deliverable management; and software/hardware management.
Operations and maintenance work (運用保守業務) is not simple work that even a first-year in-house SE can do; it is essential for the company's IT to operate normally in daily business.

For in-house SEs, operations and maintenance is a chance to acquire broad knowledge of both business and systems, and an excellent opportunity to expand personal networks by interacting with various people.
Issues that arise in operations and maintenance serve as practical material for developing problem-solving skills.
There are various roles within operations and maintenance; first-year in-house SEs need to understand the related terminology.
システム運用 (System Operations): work necessary to keep systems running, such as log monitoring and alert confirmation.
システム保守 (System Maintenance): system modification work such as version upgrades and bug fixes.
業務運用保守 (Business Operations Maintenance): receiving and responding to requests and inquiries that occur in business operations.
サービスデスク (Service Desk): a primary reception window that accepts all inquiries regardless of business domain or IT domain.
ヘルプデスク (Help Desk): a highly specialized window for system operations etc.; the service desk receives user inquiries and coordinates with specialized help desks for each system.
These role divisions are general definitions; in some companies the same team may handle several of the roles.
Operations and maintenance work is a way to build networks (人脈を構築する).
Organizational IT operations and maintenance structures vary by company, so the general model (Figure 3-3) must be used as a baseline to understand each firm's actual functional placement of roles.
End-to-end issue/request handling starts when a business user detects a problem or need and routes it to 業務運用保守 (business operations and maintenance).
業務運用保守 performs 切り分け (triage/classification): IT-related items go to the ITヘルプデスク (IT help desk) for インシデント (incident) registration; non-IT items are routed elsewhere.
The IT help desk forwards registered incidents to 運用保守 (IT operations and maintenance), which may collaborate with an 運用保守SIer (operations/maintenance system integrator) to resolve them.
After resolution, the answer is returned along the chain to the original inquirer and finally to the business user (問い合わせ → 切り分け → 対応 → 解消連絡).

HR, payroll, and similar non-IT business requests go to the サービスデスク (service desk), which registers an incident and coordinates with the relevant departmental team; in some firms the IT department itself operates the service desk.
The flow diagram (Figure 3-4) shows parallel paths: IT issues travel User → 業務運用保守 → Help Desk → 運用保守; non-IT issues travel User → Service Desk → relevant business department (e.g., 経理, 営業).
Key organizational actors include 業務ユーザー, 業務運用保守, ITヘルプデスク, 運用保守, サービスデスク, and various business departments, with optional SIer support for technical resolution.

運用保守 (operations and maintenance) is an opportunity-rich area of work for first-year in-house SEs (社内SE 1年生) to efficiently acquire knowledge and skill up; missing this chance for growth is not an option.

① Knowledge expansion (知識を広げる): Service desk assignment involves inquiries across many domains, giving a chance to learn not only IT but also the company's business and business processes. The pretext of answering inquiries makes it easier to interview domain experts (有識者).

② Network expansion (ネットワークを広げる): Operations work creates contact with inquiring users and with experts needed for problem solving. It is both a chance to know others and for others to know you. Solo skill-up has limits; building a network and knowing people who know people applies leverage to what you can do. Network is your asset (財産).

③ Problem-solving skill (課題解決力を磨く): Operations brings many issues; handling them polishes problem-solving skill and is a chance to apply conceptual skills (コンセプチュアルスキル) in practice. Abilities gained in this period help later in projects and problem-solving situations.
Key statement: 運用保守はチャンスの宝庫 (operations and maintenance is a treasure trove of opportunities).
Practical advice: Carry out 運用保守業務 and thereby gain trust (信頼を得る).

Operations/maintenance work (運用保守) for first-year in-house SEs (社内SE) contains opportunities but also stressful, challenging situations, because an inquiry to operations typically means a user is already dissatisfied.

When users show irritated attitudes, do not spend energy reacting to the attitude; set emotions aside and focus on solving the root cause. The guiding image is “hate the sin, not the sinner” (悪を憎んで人を憎まず). Reacting to attitude makes no one happier, whereas removing the cause of dissatisfaction can make everyone happier.

In-house SE work, including operations/maintenance, is teamwork. Do not try to handle every incident alone. If you lack knowledge and cannot even find a starting point, consult a supervisor, colleague, or subject-matter expert and solve it as a team.

Execute the tasks that should be done, not merely the tasks you are able to do. Processing incidents strictly in the order received risks postponing urgent incidents that need emergency response. Effective operations require starting with priority work.
Warren Buffett: “Tasks other than the ones you should do are tasks that interfere with the ones you should do.”

A four-quadrant framework (やるべきタスクを判断する4象限) judges work by importance (重要度) versus urgency (緊急度): high importance + high urgency → do immediately (今すぐやる); high importance + low urgency → plan, or ask whether it is truly important (計画する or 本当に重要かを問う); low importance + high urgency → do immediately or plan (今すぐやる or 計画する); low importance + low urgency → do not do (やらない). Important tasks must be protected from tasks that merely interfere with them.

In companies, the three core resources of people (ヒト), things/materials (モノ), and money (カネ) are managed to structure daily business and projects, with the aims of expanding sales and improving operations.
First-year in-house systems engineers (社内SE 1年生) start with project management—a limited-scope form of resource management—before taking on the larger steering of organizational operations.

Project management is the gateway (登竜門) to managing people, things, and money; the elements managed are the same for both projects and organizations, so knowledge and experience must be polished through projects.

Resources (ヒト・モノ・カネ) are allocated from the company as a whole to organizations, and from organizations onward to teams and individual projects (illustrated as allocation across organizations A/B, their teams, and projects ①–④).

Project management is not an end in itself; its purpose is to take necessary actions through management in order to lead the project to success. The same principle applies to organizational operations: management is only a means, not the goal.
To make management function as a means, appropriate information must be collected, visualized, and made available so that judgments can be formed.

Figure 3-7 lists the main project-management items that typically require active management. A first-year in-house SE (社内SE 1年生) is rarely given responsibility for every item at once, but still needs to know what the items are and how they are used.
進捗管理 (Progress management): Compare the work plan against daily actual-work information to track project progress.
リソース管理 (Resource management): Manage all personnel participating in the project, including external SIers.

予算管理 (Budget management): Track planned versus actual budget needed for project execution. Understanding internal processes such as budget approval and 稟議 (ringi) for budget disbursement is also important.
課題管理 (Issue management): Manage issues that actually arise during project progress.
リスク管理 (Risk management): Distinguish issues (already-manifested past events) from risks (future issues that have not yet occurred). Predict those risks and take avoidance measures.
マイルストーン管理 (Milestone management): Manage the planned schedule of important activities envisioned for the whole project.
コミュニケーション管理 (Communication management): Beyond weekly or monthly progress meetings, define how information is circulated to stakeholders. Its importance has risen with the spread of remote work.
成果物管理 (Deliverable management): Manage all project deliverables and meeting materials, including those produced by SIers as well as internal meeting documents.
ソフトウェア、ハードウェア管理 (Software and hardware management): Manage ancillary equipment required for system construction, such as PCs, printers, and network devices.
Subsequent pages of the chapter pick several of the above items that a first-year in-house SE should especially master and explain them in more detail.
進捗管理はプロジェクトマネジメントの重要項目であり、単なる作業管理と捉えると失敗しやすい。本質は情報を集めて眺めることではなく、予定と実績の差から課題を認識し、必要な行動を促して実行させることにある。
進捗管理の目的は「進捗を管理し、課題に対応する」ことである。
進捗管理を始める前に、プロジェクト全体計画とカギとなるマイルストーンを理解し、全体計画にアラインした担当領域の作業計画を作成して合意を得てから作業を推進する。
担当領域を正しく理解し、推進に必要な作業を自ら洗い出す。SIer提出の予定だけ実施すればうまくいくと勘違いしてはならない。SIerが担うのはSIer担当領域のみであり、社内SEが担う領域の作業は自分で洗い出す必要がある。
進捗管理のプロセスは次の流れである：プロジェクト全体計画・マイルストーンの理解 → 担当領域の理解 → 必要作業の洗い出し → 作業日程を責任者と合意 → 進捗管理 → 遅延対応。

Progress management is a means to advance a project, not an end in itself. Densely tracking progress is insufficient; one must act on delays and issues that become visible and take concrete steps to keep the project moving (e.g., delay-response actions).
Clarify owner and due date for every item. If the responsible person is unclear, ownership of progress becomes ambiguous and can end with nobody holding the ball.

Do not let each team use different progress-management tools or templates. Heterogeneous methods consume large effort on visualization and consolidation. Adopt the same tools and templates project-wide so progress can be shared and managed in a timely way.

Align on the meaning of each deliverable before work proceeds. Example: an SIer work item labeled “deliverable review” can still cause delay if parties disagree on what must be written and to what depth; the review then finds the artifact incomplete relative to expectations.

When multiple teams exist, after each team finishes task identification, jointly read through key milestones and tasks that have cross-team dependencies. A common failure is insufficient communication on cross-functional work, so neither team takes ownership and the work never starts. Actively reconcile premises and milestones with related teams.
WBS (Work Breakdown Structure) is a method used in progress management that decomposes an entire project down to the work level and manages it structurally.
WBS is commonly implemented using tools such as Excel, Jira Software, and Microsoft Project.
A WBS typically consists of tasks, planned and actual dates, assignees, progress status, and other elements that visualize the schedule (planned revision dates may be omitted in diagrams).
WBS is used to efficiently manage project progress.
WBS structures work hierarchically from large classification (大分類) through medium classification (中分類) to small classification (小分類), along with assignee, progress, and date fields.

Example WBS breakdown for 'App A development': requirements definition (including As-Is flow, To-Be flow, and requirements list), functional requirements, non-functional requirements, basic design, detailed design, and construction, with monthly schedule visualization (e.g., January through August).
Example assignees include business department A (業務部門A), internal SE B (社内SE B), and SIer C; progress statuses include completed (完了) and not yet started (未).
A key WBS practice is to first confirm templates and tools rather than creating a unique Excel WBS from scratch; use the project's common templates.
When starting WBS work, first confirm whether the project already specifies templates or tools; discovering them later creates extra transcription effort.

Do not over-focus on the visual appearance of a WBS. A WBS is a means of progress management, not a deliverable that must look beautiful. A simple WBS is easier to operate for daily task management and moving the project forward.

Identify tasks starting from large categories. Apply MECE (Mutually Exclusive and Collectively Exhaustive) from logical thinking: no omissions and no overlaps. Clarify the high-level viewpoints first, then break them down into finer tasks.

Do not assume that managing only the WBS submitted by an SIer is sufficient. An SIer typically covers only the contracted scope, not the entire internal project. The internal SE must enumerate the full set of tasks needed to drive the project, align on which areas the SIer does and does not own, and then manage and execute the whole set.

Create a realistic plan. If the WBS already shows that the schedule cannot meet the deadline, do not start work under an overtime-assumption to force the date. Escalate the issue immediately so the project can consider countermeasures. First-year internal SEs should have their WBS reviewed by a project leader because task omissions are likely.

Reuse past WBS examples. Even if WBS creation is new for a first-year internal SE, companies typically have many prior projects; finding and referring to earlier WBS structure and setup can save time.

In system development projects, systems are built through people's actions, so people are a very important element. If people with the necessary skills cannot be secured for the required time, the target output cannot be produced.

Resource management, like progress management, is not an end in itself; its purpose is to smoothly advance the project. It therefore includes not only managing resources but also optimally allocating needed resources according to the project's situation.
It is necessary to understand what resources are required for the work and to acquire the know-how for managing them.

To carry out resource management, the terms 工数 (effort/work volume), 人日 (man-day), 人月 (man-month), and FTE must be understood. SIer estimates and project conversations often express work in man-days or man-months.
工数: the amount of work required to complete a given task.
人日: the amount of work that takes one person one day; 1 man-day is calculated as 8 hours.
人月: the amount of work that takes one person one month; 1 man-month is calculated as 20 days.

FTE (Full-Time Equivalent): a measure of work rate. 1 FTE is the work rate one worker can produce in one month. Example: a task of 1 man-month takes 1 month at 1 FTE, or 0.5 months if 2 FTE are applied.
The role of resource management is to manage people in order to advance the project.
Resource management proceeds from work items identified in progress management: estimate the required effort (工数 / man-hours) for each task, then assign people to those tasks.

The flow of resource management is: (1) understand the overall project plan and milestones, (2) identify necessary work, (3) estimate required man-hours for each work item, (4) assign personnel (担当者をアサインする), (5) understand the assigned area of responsibility.
Resource management is linked to the common progress-management process.

Effort is typically estimated by project phase (要件定義 / requirements definition, 基本設計 / basic design, 開発 / development, システムテスト / system test, 受入テスト / acceptance test) and by calendar month, expressed in 人月 (man-months).

Example effort table (man-months): phases show allocations such as 要件定義 0.3 across months; 基本設計 3.7 total; 開発 4 total; monthly totals include June 3.25, July 1, August 2.5, September 3, October figures completing the plan.

Personnel assignment example maps named roles (責任者 A, PM B, 業務部門 C/D/E, 社内SE F/G, 関連部署 H) to monthly man-month allocations that sum to the phase estimates, illustrating how identified work is staffed.
Figure 3-11 visualizes both the resource-management process flow and the assignment of people to the identified work items.
First-year in-house SEs (社内SE) are rarely given full responsibility for managing an entire project's budget, but they must not be indifferent to it.
Money is one of a company's three management resources (ヒト・モノ・カネ: people, goods, and money) and functions like gasoline in a car: it is the fuel that allows a project to run.
The purpose of budget management is to ensure that funds are used without waste, do not run out, and are allocated according to plan so the project can be completed.
New team members must become able to follow typical project cost conversations such as 'How much is the license fee?' and 'What is the infrastructure cost?'
License fees (ライセンス費用): costs of using software, paid monthly or as a lump sum depending on the contract.
Cloud usage fees (クラウド利用料): costs of using cloud platforms such as AWS, separate from software; for SaaS they may be bundled into license fees.
System construction costs (システム構築費): fees paid to an SIer or similar vendor to build the system.
Network costs (ネットワーク費用): costs of building and using the network.
Operation and maintenance costs (運用保守費用): costs of keeping the completed system running.
Travel and meeting expenses (旅費、会議費): major miscellaneous project expenses that are easily forgotten in pre-project estimates and therefore require special attention.
Hardware purchase costs (ハードウェア購入費): costs of servers and other equipment needed for development.
Core principle of project budget control: 'Don't let the gasoline run dry' (ガソリンを枯れさせない) so the project can finish.

Budget consists of investment (投資) and expenses (経費); what can be booked as each slightly differs by company, so when assigned budget management you must confirm the company's definitions of investment vs. expenses.

Budget management is not mere actuals tracking. The fundamental premise is a solid plan and contracts that already specify when and how much money will be spent; only then can you notice and act on variances between plan and actuals.

Never allow an SIer to start work without a contract and without internal budget approval. Work may begin only after the proper internal approval process has been passed and a contract has been executed.

System-development contracts are either quasi-mandate (準委任契約) or lump-sum/請負 (請負契約). Under quasi-mandate you pay for the work performed: you receive a work report (typically at month-end), inspect/accept it, then pay the invoice. Under 請負 you inspect/accept the deliverable itself and then pay.
Treat the budget-management spreadsheet with extreme care. Never place it in a folder an SIer can access; if the vendor sees the budget, your negotiating position is completely exposed.
If a budget shortfall occurs, escalate immediately and do not conceal it. Money problems readily escalate into major trouble.
In any project, unexpected issues of varying size will occur; the project cannot proceed without resolving them.
The purpose of issue management (課題管理) is not merely to compile and visualize issues, but to resolve them by the required deadlines.
Core rule of issue management: manage issues and resolve them (or cause them to be resolved).
Handle issues as promptly as possible to prevent problems from spreading (“don’t let the wound widen”).
Fast response depends on two speeds: speed of recognizing an issue and speed of escalating it.
Improving recognition speed requires precursor/sign detection (予兆検知).
Driving analogy for precursor detection: a skilled driver notices irregular braking of the car ahead, infers a distracted driver, and slows down to avoid risk.

Project examples of precursor detection: an SIer that will not present a WBS may indicate insufficient development experience; an org chart of the business department may indicate a shortage of specific SMEs and thus insufficient requirements; test results with no defects at all may indicate insufficient test cases.
Record issues in an issue management table (課題管理表) so they can be listed and tracked (title, content, ticket, etc.).
Issue-management process (図3-13): issue collection → impact analysis → priority determination → implementation and follow-up.

Issue (課題) management requires at minimum tracking: expected completion date, person in charge, response content/result, impact level, and status. Managing these items is enough for issue management to function.

Issue descriptions must clearly state what the problem is. Vague wording like 'the screen freezes' is insufficient; write specifically, e.g. 'When uploading 100 or more records, the screen transitions to a white screen and becomes unresponsive,' so impact investigation is easier.
Priority rule: address high-impact issues first. Misjudging priority can let a serious issue worsen into an irrecoverable situation.

Issue follow-up: visualization is not the goal—resolution is. Persistently prompt action by the due date. If the issue is beyond one's capacity, convene a meeting of knowledgeable people or escalate to management to force action.

Exercise (today = Dec 7): Sample 1 has been open 4 days and is still incomplete. Person A wrongly prioritized completing Sample 2 (same ticket date, low impact) instead. Sample 4 is likely to stall given A's load. Reassign Sample 1 to Person B (who already finished Sample 3) to resolve the high-impact issue first.

The purpose of communication management in a project is not merely to organize information traffic and make information flow appropriately; that is only a means. The essential purpose is to make communication smooth and lead the project to success.
Communication management, though it sounds formal, simply means creating mechanisms and taking actions so that communication can proceed smoothly.
A large part of communication management is how the project manager, project leader, and PMO (Project Management Office) construct the mechanisms for communication methods.

A first-year in-house SE (社内SE 1年生) rarely participates in building those mechanisms. They are expected to grasp the overall picture of the mechanisms and then carry out the necessary communications using the necessary channels.
A common source of confusion for first-year in-house SEs is the difference between project communication and organizational communication. Both are required, not one or the other.

In a project, communication based on the project organization chart (体制図) is necessary. At the same time, even while executing the project, reporting to superiors according to the company organization chart (組織図) and 1-on-1s are also necessary.
Example: If you are a member of the development team, you need intra-team, inter-team, and project-leader reports and escalations, and you also need activity reports to your organizational superior.

It is also necessary to grasp who, what, when, where, and how to communicate. Each company has its own unique communication rules (e.g., weekly report formats, document appearance/style, document storage methods). Understand these 'how' manners (作法) and perform smooth information exchange.

Key related concepts/headings from the page: creating mechanisms for communication (コミュニケーションのための仕組み作り), the difference between project and organizational communication (プロジェクトと組織のコミュニケーションの違い), and following the communication management mechanisms (コミュニケーション管理の仕組みに従う).

In in-house SE work, communication must be planned by category of who (相手), what (内容), when/where (タイミング・場), and how (手段). A typical matrix distinguishes project communication from organizational communication.
Project-internal communication: share information with the project team at weekly standing meetings using prescribed formats; discuss content as needed by oral or written means.
Cross-team project communication: share information with other teams at weekly standing meetings using prescribed formats; discuss content as needed orally or in writing.
Reporting to the IT project leader (IT PL): report at weekly standing meetings using prescribed formats; escalate as needed orally or in writing.
Organizational communication to a supervisor: report in 1-on-1s or standing meetings using prescribed formats.
Organizational communication with colleagues: share information as needed, orally or in writing.
A core skill for first-year in-house SEs is situational choice of communication medium: decide what should be spoken and what should be written.

Oral communication emphasizes speed of information linkage. Facial expression and immediate replies make the counterpart’s reaction easy to read, so it is suited to exploring direction while communicating.
Written communication is used when accuracy matters more than timeliness, for formal agreements, or when the volume of information is too large for oral exchange.

Project communication structure typically includes: you inside the development team, IT PL, business-standardization team, project manager, project owner, steering committee, inter-team communication, and escalation/reporting paths.
Organizational communication structure is simpler: you, your boss, and the business PL (project leader). PL = プロジェクトリーダー.
Figures contrast project vs. organization communication (escalation/reporting, team-to-team, steering committee vs. boss/colleague 1-on-1s) and the oral-vs-document method split.
Deliverable management (成果物管理) is positioned as one element within communication management in IT projects.

Narrow definition of deliverables (成果物): items submitted by the SIer to the in-house SE (社内SE).
