Broad definition: not limited to final delivered items; includes regular meeting materials, kickoff materials, WBS, issue management tables (課題管理表), consideration materials, budget management tables, resource management tables, and many other documents.

Define deliverable storage rules before the project starts: specify which deliverables go where. Align with the IT department's existing deliverable management so project practices stay consistent with the organization as a whole.
Do not manage only final completed documents. Managing in-progress (working) documents is equally important in a project.

Overly strict rules on working documents can reduce work efficiency. A common practical pattern is: standardize the storage location for final deliverables across the whole project, while creating team-specific folders for working documents and leaving that area to each team's discretion.

Project-specific deliverable management rules should not be invented in isolation. The project is one of many inside the IT department; aligning methods with other projects avoids creating new, inconsistent document-management practices.
The range of items that must be managed is broad; deliverable management should therefore be systematized rather than handled ad hoc.
Folder structures in IT project management require explicit rules; they reduce the effort of deciding where things go and make overall management easier.

Recommended folder-structure rules when no company sample exists: create folders by project phase/process (工程別); define and apply file naming conventions; inside each phase folder, create subfolders by team; verify that folders have appropriate access rights.
Progress reports, budget materials, and similar management documents should use common templates so that tracking and reporting stay simple and consistent.

Document the project’s deliverable-management rules and communicate them to everyone. This is especially important on long-term projects because both the client organization and the SIer experience staff turnover that can otherwise produce inconsistencies.

Example folder layout (Figure 3-17) organizes content under a project-name root with branches such as: Planning (企画); Meeting bodies (会議体) containing status meetings (ステコミ), weekly regulars (週次定例) and team meetings; development phases (要件定義, 設計, テスト, 移行, 運用); Project management containing Progress (進捗), Resources (リソース), Budget (予算), Risk (リスク), Milestone (マイルストーン) and Communication (コミュニケーション); plus Hardware, Contract and Received materials (受領資料).

In system construction projects, a frequent trouble is lending PCs and IDs to an SIer (System Integrator) for work, after which personnel turnover inside the SIer occurs without the management ledger being updated, so it becomes unknown who holds which assets and where.
Software and hardware required for a project must be managed appropriately to avoid such troubles.

Low-value consumables such as pencils and notebooks do not need strict management, but items that constitute assets or that would create a confidentiality-leakage risk if lost (especially PCs) must be managed.

PCs lent to an SIer require management because they may be used to access important internal company information; a rule should be enforced that personnel changes inside the SIer are reported and the management ledger is updated.
IDs that grant access to internal company systems likewise require management, on the same basis as PCs.

When a project room is created and a temporary network is installed, network equipment borrowed from the infrastructure team should have its installation-through-management procedures agreed in advance with that team.
The governing principle is balanced (メリハリある) equipment management: apply strict control only to high-risk or asset-class items in order to avoid unnecessary trouble.

In operations/maintenance project management, software licenses must be actively managed—especially for restricted-license software—so that growth in project staffing does not cause license shortages.
Inexpensive supplies (備品) generally do not need micro-management. High-value items should be tracked in a management ledger (管理台帳) the same way PCs are, because of theft and resale risk.

A software/hardware management ledger typically records: category, item, management number, registration date, user, usage start date, usage end date, person in charge of management, last confirmation date, license expiration, storage location, and return deadline.
Example setup: three software licenses are owned; the ledger records who uses each license, when usage was last confirmed, and when the license expires.

Hardware example: four PCs plus one router. For each PC, record who will use it and until when. Unused PCs must have a recorded storage location. Shared equipment borrowed from another team (e.g., a router) must have a recorded return deadline.
Management-ledger columns illustrated: カテゴリ (software/hardware), 品目, 管理番号, 登録日, 利用者, 利用開始日, 利用終了日, 管理担当, 最終確認日, ライセンス期限, 保管場所, 返却期限.
IT projects are a form of manufacturing (monozukuri): without allocating the necessary people (hito), things (mono), and money (kane), the intended output cannot be obtained.
Progress management means recognizing issues from the gap between plan and actual results, prompting action, and ensuring execution.
Issue management must not stop at making issues visible; issues are collected in order to be resolved.
Operations and maintenance work is a networking opportunity: it is not only a chance for you to know others, but also for others to know you.
The purpose of project management is not management itself, but using management to prompt action and lead the project to success.
Budget management is like managing gasoline in a car: ensure the project's 'fuel' is not wasted and does not run out.
Operations and maintenance work is a critical element supporting day-to-day business, and for a first-year in-house SE it is a chance to broadly acquire knowledge of both business and systems.
From Chapter 4 onward, the book uses examples of system construction projects assigned to first-year in-house SEs (社内SE 1年生) to explain process-specific know-how.
First-year in-house SEs are rarely given end-to-end responsibility for a large-scale system construction project from start to finish.
They are more often dropped into one specific process and asked to support only part of the project.
In that situation it is easy to lose sight of how preceding and following processes connect, what the overall system-construction approach is, and what contribution is actually expected.
Chapter 4 therefore first explains the overall picture of system construction and the available approach options; these options are shown in Figure 4-1.

Questions Chapter 4 is intended to answer include: What is the overall picture of system construction? What approaches exist for carrying out system construction? What development methods are currently mainstream?
Chapter 4 frames system construction (システム構築) as a set of approach choices that sit under business strategy → IT strategy → project policy → system construction policy.

Four axes of system-construction approach choices: (1) how to do business improvement/reform, (2) how to do system construction itself, (3) how to use an SIer, (4) which development methodology to select.
Business improvement/reform options include BPR, digitalization, and DX.
System construction options include enhance (enhancement) development, scratch development, package introduction, and cloud utilization.
SIer utilization options include in-house promotion, IT support only, support on both business and IT sides, and complete outsourcing (丸投げ).
Development methodology options include waterfall, agile, and hybrid.

The chapter’s sections map to these axes: business improvement/reform approaches, system construction phases, system introduction choices, development organization choices, and development methodology choices.
In-house SE (社内SE) involvement in a project should change according to the project's aims; representative business improvement and reform methods that affect project direction must be understood.

業務改善 (business improvement) is limited to specific departments or functions: improvement issues are defined in a restricted area and the goal is to solve those issues. Examples: reviewing business flows for limited functions such as receiving or shipping; improving the order-receiving process.

BPR (Business Process Re-engineering) aims at organization-wide reform, not merely a single department or function. Examples: fundamental company-wide process redesign premised on ERP introduction; outsourcing operations via BPO (Business Process Outsourcing).

A common dilemma is that management launches a project as BPR expecting radical reform, yet the front line does not distinguish BPR from ordinary 業務改善 and consequently shrinks the project into mere incremental improvement.
デジタル化 (digitalization) applies digital technology to digitize existing operations. Examples: handling reservations online; abolishing paper-based approvals in favor of electronic ones.

DX (digital transformation) is business transformation and creation of customer value that takes digital technology as a premise. Examples: shifting sales activities online; providing online diagnosis via smartphone.

The four approaches form a spectrum from localized process tweaks (業務改善) through organization-wide redesign (BPR) and digitization of current work (デジタル化) to digitally enabled business-model change (DX).
Projects must be understood in terms of why they were launched, and contributions should match those expectations.
Business improvement (業務改善) is improvement limited to a specific business area or function; its project scope is typically a partial process within one department (e.g., department A).

BPR (Business Process Reengineering) is not confined to a single department or function; it is executed cross-organizationally across multiple departments (e.g., departments A–D). Even when limited to a domain such as manufacturing or accounting, it aims at fundamental reform of that defined area.
Digitalization (デジタル化) means applying digital technology to existing business processes.

DX (Digital Transformation) does not take existing processes as the base; it uses IT and digital technology to create new customer value and competitive advantage. Scope can include new businesses or processes that start from digital technology rather than merely overlaying digital on current processes.

Figure 4-4 contrasts four approaches: (1) partial process improvement in one department, (2) cross-departmental BPR, (3) overlaying digital on existing processes, and (4) digital-first transformation for new value.

First-year in-house SEs (社内SE 1年生) are almost never assigned to construct a large-scale system alone; they typically join from a limited work area of a specific phase of system construction, which makes the overall project picture and connections between preceding/following activities hard to see.

System construction projects (whether waterfall or agile) proceed in later stages based on matters decided in previous stages; if items that should have been decided earlier were not decided, those contents must be carried out in later stages.
First-year in-house SEs must understand the work that should be done in each stage and acquire the know-how required per stage so they can pass the baton well to subsequent stages.

Projects are largely composed of four phases: 起案フェーズ (proposal phase: plan based on strategy and turn it into a project); 立ち上げフェーズ (launch phase: organize the project and make it concrete); 構築フェーズ (construction phase: realize the system); リリース・運用フェーズ (release and operation phase: release the system and carry out daily operations).
It is important to understand role division within the project team in relation to these phases.

Example of collaboration: in system construction for improving a certain business, the business department (業務部門) performs business design, while the in-house SE collaborates with the SIer to refine requirements and specifications and jointly promote the work.
A business-improvement project in which the in-house SE alone executes everything (business design, system construction, testing, and release) should not exist.

The book covers the work necessary for system construction and the respective know-how for general roles, emphasizing proceeding through phases via collaboration (協業でフェーズを進める) and grasping the phases of system construction (システム構築のフェーズを押さえる).

System introduction methods are diverse; the chosen method affects how requirements definition and development proceed. Representative options include enhance development, scratch development, package introduction, and cloud service utilization; RPA use is also an option. Outsourcing for man-hour reduction is excluded here when the goal is not bound by business improvement via system construction.

Understanding the characteristics of each introduction method is necessary to select the optimal means for realizing in-house system construction. First-year in-house SEs must grasp these characteristics and adopt the corresponding stance and behavior for each method.

Enhance development (エンハンス開発): development of some kind against an existing system, such as modifications/repairs. Development period is generally short but depends on the complexity of the existing system. Typical projects include partial business improvement. First-year in-house SEs are often assigned responsibility for such work.

Scratch development (スクラッチ開発): an original system is developed from scratch according to requirements, by the company itself or an SIer. Development period is longer than enhance development or package introduction. Typical projects include business improvement, BPR, and digitalization.

Scratch development (スクラッチ開発) is often used when a company has an in-house development team; it is flexible because development follows requirements, but unlike packages or cloud services, specifications depend on developers, so systems easily become black boxes and operations also tend to depend on those developers.

Package introduction (パッケージ導入) means introducing existing (off-the-shelf) software; development period is shorter than scratch development; typical projects include business improvement, BPR, and digitalization.

Package and cloud-service projects are increasing; they should be driven by fitting business processes to the package rather than customizing the package to existing processes; a small-start approach is basic to keep cost and complexity down; agile methods are readily applicable.

Cloud service usage (クラウドサービス利用) means using services such as SaaS; development period is shorter than scratch development; typical projects include business improvement, BPR, and digitalization; thorough understanding of the service is extremely important, and agile methods are readily applicable.

RPA usage (RPA利用) means automation through robotic process automation technology; development period is shorter than scratch development; typical projects include business improvement, BPR, and digitalization.

RPA can often support small-scale development requests or functional improvements to existing mechanisms without full system development; organizations should check whether an internal IT RPA promotion team exists and prefer the RPA tools that team recommends.
When a company does not have its own in-house development team, projects proceed by having an external SIer (System Integrator) support system construction.

Utilization of external resources in system construction has several patterns; typical responsibility scopes (守備範囲) across phases are assigned among the business department (業務部門), in-house SE (社内SE), business consultant (業務コンサルタント), SIer, and SES.
System construction phases include proposal (起案), launch (立ち上げ), operation (運用), construction (構築), requirements definition (要件定義), development (開発), and operations/maintenance (運用保守).
Variations by company: some request the SIer to handle maintenance as well; in small-scale development, SES may be asked to support from upstream processes.
Projects combine external resources in various ways; five commonly observed patterns of external-resource utilization exist and should be understood as options for development structure (開発体制).

System construction (システム構築) can follow several patterns depending on whether and how external resources are used, illustrated in Figure 4-8 across phases such as proposal (起案), startup (立ち上げ), construction (構築) including requirements definition (要件定義) and development (開発), and operations/maintenance (運用保守).
Pattern ① is in-house development (自社開発のモデル) that does not use external resources.
Pattern ② is typical of relatively small-to-medium-scale projects: the company solidifies requirements internally and commissions development to an SIer.
Pattern ③ is used for large-scale projects: business consultants (業務コンサルタント) support from the proposal phase to solidify planning, then an SIer is used.
Patterns ④ and ⑤ must be avoided. They occur when a project starts as ① or ② but ends up as complete dumping of responsibility (丸投げ).
If a project falls into pattern ④ or ⑤, escalate to the project manager that original roles are not functioning and that fundamental countermeasures are required.
Pattern ④: the business department (業務部門) abandons consideration and dumps it on the internal SE (社内SE) and SIer; the result is almost always a system that is never used.

Pattern ⑤: the business department dumps work on business consultants, and the internal SE dumps both consideration and development on the SIer without even follow-up; this wastes money and time and produces either an unused system or nothing at all.
Key parties whose involvement varies by pattern and phase include the business department, internal SE, SIer, and business consultants.
There are three methodologies for system development; the approach to requirements definition, testing, release, and related activities differs by methodology.

Waterfall development proceeds through processes one by one: the next process starts only after the previous process is completed. It is characterized by easy process management, strong quality control, and ease of planning. Typical practice is to solidify requirements, obtain estimates from an SIer, and then begin development.

Typical Waterfall phases include requirements analysis (要求分析), requirements definition (要件定義), basic design (基本設計), detailed design (詳細設計), programming (プログラミング), unit testing (単体テスト), integration testing (結合テスト), system testing (システムテスト), and acceptance testing (受入テスト).

Agile development breaks work into small development units and aims for speedy release. Compared with Waterfall, it produces fewer deliverables and proceeds by repeating cycles of development, testing, and release.

Agile is suitable for some domains and not others. Web-related development often uses Agile to accelerate releases and deliver value to users quickly. It is less suited to domains such as warehouse operations that involve physical on-site work.
Hybrid development (ハイブリッド開発) is an approach in which the entire project is not run as Agile; Waterfall is used only for selected portions of the work.

One hybrid model plans requirements definition (要件定義) and basic design (基本設計) in a Waterfall style, while the SIer-performed system construction proceeds in Agile; testing is then performed in reasonably sized batches with the goal of release.

Warehouse and similar physical systems are often better suited to Waterfall: daily Agile development and release would force corresponding daily warehouse-layout changes, which operations cannot absorb.

The V-model hybrid development (V字モデルのハイブリッド開発) pairs Waterfall-style early phases (requirements analysis, basic design) with later Agile cycles of development, testing, and release (including integration test, system test, and acceptance test).
System introduction options include enhance development (エンハンス開発), scratch development (スクラッチ開発), package introduction (パッケージ導入), cloud service utilization (クラウドサービス利用), and RPA utilization (RPA 利用).
Development methodologies include Waterfall, Agile, and Hybrid; understand the assigned project's methodology and prepare to contribute according to its progress.
Agile development breaks development units into small pieces and aims for early release; it tends to produce fewer deliverables than Waterfall.

First-year in-house SEs often provide spot support across the four project phases (proposal/起案, launch/立ち上げ, construction/構築, release and operation/リリース・運用) and tend to lose the overall picture, so they must respond with awareness of connections between phases.
Projects can be classified by whether external resources are used, into patterns such as in-house development (自社開発) and SIer utilization.
Waterfall development proceeds one process at a time after the previous process is completed; it offers easy process management, excellent quality control, and ease of planning.
Differences in business improvement and reform methods greatly affect how a project proceeds; know the assigned project's method and aim for contributions that meet expectations.

A common claim is that the success or failure of system construction is decided by requirements definition (要件定義), because upstream process choices are reflected in implementation; this view is primarily an SIer (system integrator) perspective.
From an in-house SE (社内SE) perspective, even if requirements definition produces a negative outcome, that is only a system-implementation failure and is not an essential project failure.

The purpose of a project is contribution to the business; therefore an idea that is never realized and never becomes a project (never even challenged) is a more fundamental problem than later delivery issues.

Real failure in system construction is when an idea is not materialized and thus receives no investment; this is distinct from implementation-side problems such as insufficiently packed requirements or systems that are built but unused.
The first step of idea realization is the proposal (起案) phase, which precedes project launch (立ち上げ); subsequent stages include requirements definition, development/testing, and delivery.
Chapter 5 addresses the flow of the proposal phase, role division in that phase, and the work that must be completed before a project is launched.
The project proposal (起案) phase is extremely important for business companies (事業会社).

First-year in-house SEs (社内SE 1年生) are typically not given full responsibility for the entire proposal phase immediately; they must understand how the phase proceeds and how it affects the overall project so they can provide support when involved on a spot basis.

Typical proposal-phase flow: in the previous fiscal year, each organization or team considers measures (施策) based on corporate strategy; super-rough estimates (超概算) are prepared; items are prioritized by cost-effectiveness (費用対効果) and importance; then the projects to be promoted and their budgets for the new year are decided.

High-level process sequence: formulate organizational strategy based on company-wide strategy → plan measures based on that strategy → rank measures by feasibility and expected effects → select the projects to promote and secure next-year budget → launch and drive the projects.
Previous-year activities typically include project-case approval, measure consideration, budget estimation, measure proposal, and strategy formulation, after which the new fiscal year begins.

In the proposal/initiation phase (起案フェーズ), the final required deliverable is the proposal document (企画書). Creating it involves organizing various information, making the proposal idea concrete, and connecting it to project launch.
Proposal document (企画書) formats are often predefined by companies using internal systems or Excel templates.
The proposal creation process should be understood; Chapter 5 explains the required inputs along the following items and process steps.
Key process steps for building the proposal: ① 施策検討 (measure/policy consideration), ② 業務検討 (business consideration), ③ システム検討 (system consideration), ④ プロジェクト計画 (project planning).

Required inputs for the proposal (企画書に必要なインプット) include: 起案部門 (proposing department), 課題一覧 (list of issues), As-Is 業務フロー (current-state business flow), 解決する課題特定 (identification of issues to solve), 業務取り組み概要 (overview of business initiatives), To-Be 業務フロー (future-state business flow), システム要求 (system requirements), システム外費用 (non-system costs), 想定効果 (expected effects/benefits), プロジェクトマイルストーン (project milestones), 体制 (organization/staffing), システム概要 (system overview), システム費用 (system costs), and 社内SE (internal systems engineer).
The proposal document is the final artifact that consolidates these inputs from business, system, and project-planning perspectives.
The proposing department (起案部門), not the internal SE (社内SE), is the party responsible for creating the project proposal document (企画書).

When a business department approaches an internal SE requesting introduction of a specific system, they often skip defining the true project purpose so that systemization itself becomes the goal rather than a means; this must be avoided.

Systemization should not be considered until the proposing department has prepared; proceeding without the proposer’s own analysis makes the purpose of the system unclear and puts the cart before the horse (本末転倒).
Standard planning sequence: (1) Consider measures — collect issues from As-Is business flows or existing services and identify those that must be solved according to corporate strategy.

Standard planning sequence: (2) Advance business consideration — design To-Be business flows, derive and organize system requirements, estimate non-system budgets, and quantify expected benefits of resolving the issues.
Standard planning sequence: (3) Consider systemization — determine how the system will solve the identified issues, ensuring alignment with the IT department’s strategy and roadmap.

Standard planning sequence: (4) Create the project plan — only after both the proposing department’s and the internal SE’s analyses have matured should the required organization/structure and high-level milestones be decided.
Deciding organization and milestones before deciding what the project will actually do commonly produces resource shortages or unrealistic plans.
As-Is/To-Be業務フローは業務の流れを図式化したものであり、As-Is業務フローは現在の業務を可視化した図、To-Be業務フローは未来の想定業務を可視化した図である。
業務フローは、業務改善ポイントの洗い出し、未来の想定業務の検討、ユーザートレーニング時の机上説明などに使用される。
起案フェーズでは、To-Be業務フローからどの業務プロセス部分をシステム化して改善できるかを検討する。
As-Is/To-Be業務フローの作成主体は基本的に業務ユーザーであり、社内SEは業務部門の作成を支援する役割を担う。
よくある失敗として、社内SEが業務フローを作成して責任まで負わされるケースや、起案フェーズからいきなり詳細化して全体感を押さえられないケースがある。
誰が・いつ・どの粒度まで業務フローを準備するかを事前に決める必要がある。
業務フローには粒度が存在し、起案フェーズ・立ち上げフェーズ・構築フェーズそれぞれで成果物が登場し、プロジェクト進行に伴い詳細化・掘り下げていく。
起案フェーズではハイレベル（抽象度の高い）業務フローを検討し、立ち上げフェーズで詳細化を進め、構築フェーズでさらに詳細まで落とし込む。
前工程での検討が甘いと、後工程で粒度の粗い業務フローをベースに詳細化しなければならなくなる。

In the project proposal (起案) phase, high-level As-Is/To-Be business process flows (業務フロー) should be created; if the proposer proceeds without documenting them, the internal SE should prompt documentation as soon as noticed.

The business department owns business-flow creation and remains responsible for it; the internal SE acts only as a support role and may create a draft or assist when that helps the project move smoothly.
Reuse existing in-house business-flow documents: match notation, legends, and style so later sharing and maintenance are easier.

Have business users produce one sample flow early and review it; capability cannot be judged from writing rules alone. If they cannot write flows at all, reconsider the overall timeline or ask a manager whether an internal training group exists.
Business-flow detailing is performed across phases (proposal/起案, launch/立ち上げ, construction/構築); the proposal phase focuses on high-level As-Is/To-Be views rather than detailed notation.
ITソリューション検討とは、業務ユーザーの要求に基づき、課題をどのようにITで解消できるか（How）を検討することである。
ITソリューション検討は、システム要求、プロジェクトの目的、IT戦略、ITロードマップ、既存システムランドスケープなどのポイントを加味して行う必要がある。
業務ユーザーが「XXXシステムがほしい！」などと要求してくる場合があるが、これは間違った要求である。システムの提案は社内SEが行う。
社内SEは、ユーザーのどんな課題を解決するための要求なのかを確認する必要がある。
ITソリューション検討の確認ポイント：どのような課題を解決しようとしているか／要求が本来の目的にそっているか／IT戦略やITロードマップとの整合性は／提案するシステムは既存のシステムランドスケープと整合するか。
検討にはシステム構築の選択肢の提案も含まれる（図5-5 ITソリューション検討のポイント）。
When making a project proposal, evaluate options using business merits/demerits, system merits/demerits, approximate 5-year total investment cost, and expected delivery time (納期).

Project purpose must be understood in parallel with requirements: DX, BPR and other improvement methods change the scope of possible measures; confirm that the project's aim is consistent with the understood requirements.

Never propose a system based only on received requirements. Proposals must pursue overall (not partial) optimization and therefore require understanding of the organization's IT strategy and IT roadmap.

Example of strategy alignment: if corporate policy is moving to the cloud, an on-premises solution that technically meets the stated requirements still requires careful scrutiny of whether it is truly the right answer.

Designing a new system solely from the current request produces siloed systems. After receiving requirements, check consistency with the existing system landscape; better alignment simplifies operations and suppresses cost.

A typical proposal table compares four options: (1) modify existing system (small business change, but aging will force migration in X years), (2) introduce a package (large business change + standardization, package selection required), (3) use SaaS (large business change + standardization, possible integrated operations with other domains), (4) RPA (covers only ~50 % of business requirements). Each row shows corresponding system implications, 5-year cost and lead time.
IT departments should propose which solution is most appropriate; what is prioritized determines the system's overall direction.

Focus on mechanisms that contribute to the business: systems that support repetitive work performed by many people, not merely 'scratch-an-itch' tools for specific users or tasks. Niche tools are not always bad if they show cost-effectiveness and fit the IT strategy/roadmap, but they are not the main path.
First-year in-house SEs participating in IT solution discussions often fall into local (individual) optimization; they must be careful to avoid this.

Business companies tend to produce locally optimized or siloed systems because of their structure: business units often have more discretion and voice than IT, and those units are themselves fragmented domestically and internationally.
In-house SEs must understand this silo-prone structure and ask whether a business-unit request has already been addressed elsewhere or can be integrated with other departments.
Siloed construction: each business unit (and overseas units) builds its own systems independently (e.g., systems A–E for units A–E).
Desired approach: integrate initiatives across units (domestic and overseas) into a shared IT platform rather than separate systems.
Same-company similar business models and processes should be candidates for integration rather than duplicated systems.
From a systems-support viewpoint, requirements can often be integrated rather than spawning isolated solutions; this is a core way to prevent siloing (サイロ化).
Check IT strategy and IT roadmap: extend the time horizon into the future and confirm the direction the organization as a whole is heading before proposing a new system.
Check whether existing or planned systems already address similar requirements (past projects or current pipelines). If yes, additional licenses or reuse may suffice instead of a new silo.

Think at group/company-wide scope: look for mechanisms usable across the whole organization, not only inside one’s own IT unit; coordinate with related companies and overseas IT organizations to optimize IT solutions.

Do not take user requirements at face value. User departments are often unclear about what they truly need from a system; the internal SE, as an IT professional, must understand the real desired outcomes and problems to be solved, then propose accordingly.

First-year internal SEs have limited knowledge and experience; do not try to design mechanisms alone. Use supervisors and project managers, and build business-contributing systems as a team rather than solving everything solo.

Siloing is avoided by combining future-oriented strategy checks, reuse of existing systems, group-wide thinking, deep inquiry into real user needs, and team consultation rather than isolated local solutions.
In-house SE (社内SE) contributes to projects from the IT side; they need not take on everything dumped by proposers, including work the proposer themselves should consider.
If in-house SE absorbs that work, the proposing department is only avoiding its own issues via manpower rather than solving them at the root.
Staff shortages may stem from how the organization allocates priorities, or from weak hiring power (company appeal and branding).
To keep the organization functioning, clearly separate what in-house SE should do from what the proposer should do, and proceed with the proposal (起案) phase on that basis.

A former boss of the author would reject unprepared business units in the proposal phase with “If you haven’t even considered it, this is a waste of time—come back after you’ve thought it through.” Most people cannot take that hard line, so a milder approach is needed.
The proposal phase involves a limited number of people, so do not rigidly apply full project-management methods or heavy deliverable definitions.
Without any defined deliverables or milestones, meetings alone waste time.

The key is for in-house SE to lay some rails for the business department: understand what must be done in the proposal phase, explain the process, schedule the tasks, and prompt the necessary considerations.
In-house SEs who can support proposers’ thinking in this way will be increasingly needed as IT demand spreads across more domains and they become the hub of those IT considerations.
Purpose of role division in the proposal phase is to be understood via five steps (役割分担の目的 / 5つのステップ / 起案フェーズの役割分担を理解する).
Internal SEs (社内SE) must proactively lay the rails (set structure and process) for project initiation with business departments, because those departments often lack project experience.
Step 1: Use self-introduction to understand the counterpart. Business-department staff may be project amateurs even after 5–10 years in the department; assess how much support they will need.

Step 2: Confirm internal processes and deadlines before planning begins (e.g., next-fiscal-year project-application cutoff). This determines the required speed of consideration; verify with a superior.

Step 3: Assess the current state of consideration in the business department (it may already be advanced or still rudimentary). Identify the proposer and the necessary next actions. In the first meeting, check status against the inputs required for the proposal document (shown in Figure 5-3).

Step 4: Accelerate consideration by requesting a ‘tatakidai’ (rough draft / straw-man). Set a sharing deadline. A draft has a much lower creation hurdle than a formal deliverable. The proposal phase involves repeated trial-and-error, so treat outputs as drafts to keep momentum.

If a proposer fails to produce even the agreed draft by the deadline, stop. Forcing the initiation phase through will likely produce the same failure in later phases. Execution ability is required to run a project; halt before the project officially starts.
Step 5: Once draft-making is agreed, schedule regular meetings (定例会). Regular meetings reduce one-off scheduling overhead and give the proposer a cadence to progress against.

In business-department-initiated projects involving internal SEs, the proposing department must always drive certain areas of the work; the IT department should not be expected to execute the entire project on its own even if the share of IT-related consideration varies.
A project’s measures consist of an IT domain that is only a subset of the whole plus non-IT measures; progress requires advancing both, not treating IT as the entirety of the project.
The subject (owner) of the project remains the proposing department; when that department is a business unit, IT and non-IT actions are mixed and both must be pursued.
A common misconception (illustrated as the right-hand side of Figure 5-8) is that the IT domain fills 100 % of the project’s measures, leading people to dump all work onto the IT department.
The underlying cause of the misconception is low IT literacy among internal staff; internal SEs should therefore help raise that literacy rather than simply absorb the dumped work.
Figure 5-8 contrasts the correct project structure (IT as only part of the measures) with the mistaken structure (IT occupying the entire project).
Japanese companies often struggle to keep up with the rapid pace of IT evolution because many lack personnel who can provide IT education.

Japan's lifetime employment system (終身雇用制度) still results in relatively low talent mobility compared with overseas, even though job-type employment (ジョブ型雇用) has increased. Consequently, business- or operations-department staff who have already run multiple projects are rarely recruited into similar projects at other companies.
High-IT-literacy talent inside a company is limited, so education that raises IT literacy is important.
Once the direction of a system introduction becomes clear, the internal SE (社内SE) should help raise IT literacy. Two practical methods are recommended.

Method 1 – Learn at solution seminars: When the introduction direction is visible, encourage attendance at seminars run by leading solutions in that domain. For packages or SaaS, the implementing SIer or package vendor typically holds regular seminars. Both the internal SE and the proposing department's staff should attend together.

Method 2 – Learn from companies that have already implemented: Many firms have already solved similar problems. If they are in a different industry they are not competitors and often willingly give lectures. If no personal connections exist, acquaintances made with package vendors at the seminars in Method 1 can provide introductions.
A first-year internal SE is almost never expected to steer these two methods, but as one advances to project-manager or higher roles such initiatives become necessary.
When assigned to a system-introduction project in an unfamiliar domain, it is highly effective for an internal SE to apply independently to relevant seminars early in order to raise domain knowledge.
超概算見積もり (ultra-rough estimate) is the process of calculating a broad, high-level budget required for a project.
First-year in-house SEs are almost never asked to produce ultra-rough estimates, but preparing for them from the first year is still valuable.
Ultra-rough estimates are based on personal experience used to secure a budget; first-year in-house SEs lack that experience, so estimation viewpoints are provided instead.

Development-cost viewpoints for ultra-rough estimates include: system license fees (package or SaaS usage fees); system construction fees paid to an SIer; interface-design costs for linking with existing systems; tester costs for outsourcing system tests (e.g., to SES); and various infrastructure-construction costs needed to build the system.
Operation-cost viewpoints for ultra-rough estimates include: various infrastructure costs (cloud usage fees, server maintenance, etc.) and post-release operation/maintenance costs.
Figure 5-9 organizes these viewpoints into 開発コスト (development costs) and 運用コスト (operation costs) as a practical framework for producing an ultra-rough project budget.
When using SaaS, construction costs may be kept low, but running (operational) costs can exceed those savings and must be considered in the estimate.
For large-scale projects, a certain amount of travel and transportation expenses should be included in the cost estimate.
A buffer (contingency/reserve fund, 予備費) for unexpected situations should be added to the estimate; the amount is decided in consultation with the project owner.
System modification projects are relatively easy to estimate because quotes can be obtained by inquiring with the existing vendor.
Introducing a new mechanism or system is much harder to estimate than modifying an existing one.
Combining multiple sources of estimate information (the options below) can raise the accuracy of the overall estimate.

Estimate-information options (図5-10): ① Web price search — package or SaaS prices can sometimes be confirmed on the web; ② Consult third-party organizations — use reporting-service companies or consulting firms; ③ Interview internal experts — if the company already has an implementation, ask the person in charge; ④ Estimate from own experience — rough calculation based on personal experience (high hurdle for a first-year internal SE, becomes possible with accumulated experience); ⑤ Direct inquiry to vendors — sales activity starts from the moment of inquiry, so timing must be adjusted.
Caveat on option ④: without relevant experience the figure is merely a guess, not a reliable estimate.
Caveat on option ⑤: communicating with vendors risks triggering unnecessary sales activity; inquiry timing must therefore be carefully coordinated.
Internal approval processes (社内承認プロセス) must be carefully sequenced and planned; otherwise they consume unexpected time and drag down the project.
The most important starting point is how the approval process is perceived: treating it as a wasteful formality prevents it from being used productively.

Some approval steps may have become hollow or ritualized, but their essential function is a company checkpoint (関所) that communicates the concept to the right people, secures budget, and obtains a GO sign to proceed.
A first-year in-house SE attending an approval judgment meeting (承認判定会議) should prepare all necessary information openly and approach the meeting wanting problems to be pointed out.

Approval meetings should be viewed positively as a project health-check; obtaining the approver’s endorsement (お墨付き) lets the project proceed with confidence, so the meeting should be treated as borrowing the approver’s support (胸を借りる).
Actual approval processes differ by company; required content and precision also differ by project phase, so the expected level of detail at each gate must be understood in advance.

In the proposal/initiation phase (起案フェーズ) measures and budget figures are still rough and high-level; this is expected, and failing to recognize it leads to spending excessive time on premature concretization.

In the proposal (起案) phase, proposed measures are deliberated from IT strategy and cost-effectiveness viewpoints to decide whether consideration should be promoted. Approving measures that diverge from strategy or lack expected effects prevents effective allocation of people, goods, and money (ヒト・モノ・カネ) in the organization. At this stage, both measure content and budget are typically rough estimates.

In the launch (立ち上げ) phase, measure content is fleshed out, cost-effectiveness is scrutinized, and whether the project should actually be started is deliberated. Confirmation that preparations such as organizational structure (体制) are in place is also performed.
In the construction (構築) phase, unexpected changes arise as the project proceeds. This phase deliberates whether to approve those changes (e.g., budget or development-scope changes).

Nemawashi (根回し) is prior information sharing needed to advance the approval process. Sharing information with the right people before the approval-judgment meeting to raise review accuracy is acceptable. Having approvers identify issues in advance, correcting them, and then attending the meeting is also acceptable. Because the approval process exists as a checkpoint (関所) to make the project meaningful, activities that raise project quality should be recommended.

Approval content by phase (各フェーズにおける承認内容): Proposal (起案) — judge promotion of measures from strategy consistency and cost-effectiveness; timing: annual; measure precision: concept/rough; budget precision: estimate/rough. Launch (立ち上げ) — judge whether to start the project after making measures concrete; timing: at project start; measure precision: outline/high; budget precision: estimate/high. Construction (構築) — approve changes to budget or development scope; timing: as needed (随時); measure precision: specific; budget precision: N/A.
Decide who, when, and to what granularity business process flows (業務フロー) will be prepared; then the internal SE supports the business department in creating those flows.
Before project start, raise internal IT literacy via training on the planned system and hearings with companies that have already implemented it.
The approval process is a checkpoint (関所): convey the concept to the right people in the company, secure budget, obtain the GO sign, and then proceed with the project.
Beware of skipping the project's original purpose that should be examined, so that systemization (the means) does not become the purpose itself.
IT solution consideration must not only meet users' functional requirements; it must comprehensively factor in IT strategy, the existing system landscape, and similar constraints.
Requirements tend to silo. Check whether the same requirement is already being handled by another department, and whether the case can be integrated with other departments' work.
For an internal SE, the real failure is when a case is never even made into a project and is never considered at all.

The 立ち上げフェーズ (project launch/initiation phase) is a critical process after requirements definition that determines the actual direction of system construction; preparation in this phase can make or break the subsequent construction phase.

In the launch phase, the project's system-construction direction is set, including rules, governance, organizational structure (体制), the system itself, SIer involvement, and role assignments, before actual system building begins.
Figure 6-1 (立ち上げフェーズの重要性) illustrates that the launch phase decides the direction of system construction and feeds that direction, along with rules and governance, into later phases.
